readings.whatItDoes:
This keeps ₱10 billion alive. Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 22 had appropriated that sum from the 2020 and 2021 Special Development Fund; this act rewrites its cash budgeting section so the money stayed releasable and disbursable to the end of 2023.

The deadlines are staged the way capital spending actually works: infrastructure could be obligated to 31 December 2023, with construction completed, inspected and paid by 30 June 2024; other items obligated to the same date with delivery and payment by 31 March 2024.

Unlike the general appropriations extensions, there is no carve-out for Personnel Services here — the Special Development Fund is a development pot rather than an operating budget, so there is no payroll in it to protect.
readings.whyProposed: A very large development programme, appropriated across two budget years in a government still building its delivery capacity, was about to lapse with works unfinished.
whoIsAffected: Communities whose roads, buildings and facilities were funded from the Special Development Fund.
Contractors mid-delivery.
Ministries and offices administering the fund.
Bangsamoro taxpayers, given the size of the sum.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, authorised to issue guidelines for the cash budgeting system

funding.detail: No new appropriation. It extends the ₱10,000,000,000 already appropriated by BAA 22 from the 2020 and 2021 Special Development Fund.

whatChanges: ₱10 billion of development money stayed usable through 2023 instead of lapsing.
Infrastructure gained a completion and payment window to 30 June 2024.
Other capital and operating items gained a window to 31 March 2024.
readings.insight:
The Special Development Fund is the largest single pot of money encountered anywhere in this registry, and it is worth understanding why it keeps needing rescue. Ten billion pesos appropriated across 2020 and 2021 — a period covering the pandemic and the earliest years of a government still assembling its procurement and engineering capacity — was never going to be spent on an annual cash budgeting cycle. Extension was the realistic alternative to mass lapse and re-appropriation.

What makes this act worth reading alongside its successor is what came next. This one still sets outer limits: obligate by the end of 2023, pay by mid-2024. A year later BAA 51 extended the same fund again and dropped the payment deadline altogether, making the money disbursable 'until fully expended'. The chain from BAA 22 to 34 to 51 is a fair record of how a hard budget constraint became a soft one, one act at a time.

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the rulebook for how the Bangsamoro elects its own parliament. Before it, the region had no election law of its own — the Bangsamoro Organic Law required one, and this Code is it.

It sets the shape of an 80-member Parliament: half the seats go to party representatives elected region-wide, 40 percent to district representatives elected by their own districts, and 10 percent — at least 8 seats — are reserved for sectors. Those reserved seats are named: two each for Non-Moro Indigenous Peoples and for settler communities, and one each for women, youth, traditional leaders, and the 'Ulama. A voter who belongs to more than one of those sectors may register in up to three of them.

It also builds the machinery around the vote. It establishes the Bangsamoro Electoral Office as COMELEC's arm in the region, and a Bangsamoro Registration and Accreditation Committee to register and accredit regional political parties, subject to COMELEC en banc approval. Parties must meet standards to register, and candidates for the reserved seats must be certified by the relevant ministry on the basis of a track record of advocacy for that sector, then declare their sector under oath.

The Code is written to push politics away from personalities and towards parties: it says so directly, instructing that where a provision is ambiguous, the reading that strengthens party-based parliamentary politics wins.
readings.whyProposed: The Bangsamoro Organic Law obliges the region to enact its own electoral code, and no parliamentary election could be held without one. Members debating it framed it as more than compliance: the first election law written for a parliamentary system in the Philippines, and the instrument that would let the first Bangsamoro parliamentary election proceed.
whoIsAffected: Every registered voter in the BARMM, who will vote for party, district, and sectoral representatives under a system that did not exist before.
Regional political parties, which must register and be accredited, and meet the Code's standards to field candidates.
Non-Moro Indigenous Peoples, settler communities, women, youth, traditional leaders, and the 'Ulama — the six groups holding reserved seats.
Anyone seeking a seat: district candidates face a one-year residency requirement, and sectoral nominees must be certified and must swear to their sector.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections (COMELEC), which retains authority over the conduct of elections and approves party accreditation en banc
Bangsamoro Electoral Office (BEO), COMELEC's office in the region, whose organisational structure and staffing COMELEC determines
Bangsamoro Registration and Accreditation Committee (BRAC), which registers and accredits regional political parties
The ministries and regional agencies that certify sectoral candidates, which were given 120 days from promulgation to issue their certification guidelines
Local governments, which continue to fund election boards, canvassing, forms, and voting centres

funding.detail: The Code carries no appropriation of its own. The BEO's budget forms part of COMELEC's yearly budget, and the Bangsamoro Parliament may add to it — the Code provides for an election reserve fund in an election year, including for the assemblies that elect sectoral representatives. Local governments keep paying for election boards, forms, paraphernalia, and voting centres.

whatChanges: The region gains an election law of its own, making a Bangsamoro parliamentary election legally possible for the first time.
8 seats are set aside for sectors that would otherwise have to win an ordinary contest to be represented.
Half of Parliament is elected by party rather than by locality, which shifts campaigning towards platforms and party lists.
Regional parties acquire a registration and accreditation process, and a body to run it.
Ministries acquire a new duty: certifying that a sectoral candidate genuinely represents that sector.
deliberation: MP Alamia voted yes but said she would keep pressing for wider inclusion of women and marginalised sectors inside regional political parties.
MP Maglangit voted yes while recording a reservation: she believes in wider and bigger representation of women in Parliament than the Code provides.
MP Arnado gave four reasons for her vote, singling out the anti-political-dynasty provision as the first of its kind in the country, and a provision discouraging non-biodegradable campaign materials.
MP Basman argued the Code cements women's participation in practical terms, noting it requires a concrete women's agenda before a party can register.
MP Ali, Jr. noted the Code went through a series of consultations with COMELEC, and that it would enable the first parliamentary election in the region in 2025.

MP Alih framed it as asymmetry made real — a system built for the region rather than copied from the national one — and cited the 30 percent women requirement in party representation and the anti-dynasty provision.
Passed on Third and Final Reading by nominal voting, 64 in favour, none against, no abstentions (Journal No. 21, 7 March 2023).
readings.insight: The reserved seats are the part to watch. 8 seats out of eighty is a floor, not a ceiling, and the Code hands the ministries a gatekeeping role — a sectoral candidate needs a certification of advocacy before standing. That makes the certification guidelines, due within 120 days of promulgation, as consequential as the seat count itself: they decide who is allowed to claim a sector. The other thing to watch is that the Code says out loud which way to resolve ambiguity — towards party-based politics — which is unusual, and tells you what its drafters expected to be argued about.

readings.whatItDoes:
This solves a specific and very ordinary injustice: a worker doing a job in the Bangsamoro, on a programme paid for by the national government, going unpaid because the money has not yet come down from Manila.

The act puts a billion pesos in a revolving fund. When a national transfer is delayed, the Bangsamoro ministry supervising the programme asks the finance ministry to release from the Fund, and the worker is paid on time. When the national agency eventually transfers the money, the Fund is reimbursed immediately and stands ready for the next delay.

Two guardrails come with it. Section 5 says plainly that none of this makes the Bangsamoro Government responsible for the National Government's obligations — the Fund covers timing, not liability, and ministries must still do whatever is needed to get the national funds released. And Section 9 requires a quarterly report on every release, obligation and disbursement, going to Parliament through the Speaker.
readings.whyProposed: The policy section frames it as protecting workers' welfare, and names the gap exactly: personnel deployed in the region under nationally funded programmes, needing a mechanism that ensures timely payment for services already rendered.
whoIsAffected: Workers and personnel on nationally-funded programmes directly supervised by Bangsamoro ministries, agencies or offices.
Those ministries, which request releases and must pursue the national downloading.
The Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, which administers the Fund and reports on it.
Parliament, through quarterly reports and the Committee on Finance, Budget and Management.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, which administers the Fund, releases on request, operates the reimbursement mechanism, issues the rules and reports quarterly
BARMM ministries, agencies and offices implementing nationally-funded programmes

funding.detail: ₱1,000,000,000 appropriated as a revolving fund, chargeable against the Contingent Fund. Because it is reimbursed whenever national funds arrive, the billion is a working balance rather than an annual cost.

whatChanges: Delayed national transfers no longer mean delayed wages for workers in the region.
A standing billion-peso facility exists for the purpose, replenished by reimbursement.
Parliament receives quarterly accounts of its use.
The Fund cannot be quietly wound up — it survives programme discontinuance and dissolves only after two fiscal years of disuse.
readings.insight:
This is a devolution act disguised as a budget mechanism. The Bangsamoro cannot make the national government pay on time; what it can do is stand between the delay and the worker, and then get its money back. That is a modest legal idea with a large practical effect, and it is aimed at exactly the people least able to absorb a late paycheque.

The drafting is unusually careful in three places. Section 5 forecloses the obvious risk — that a bridging fund becomes a permanent subsidy, with national agencies content to let the region carry their payroll — by stating in terms that the Bangsamoro Government assumes none of the National Government's responsibilities. Section 6 forecloses the opposite risk, that the Fund is dissolved the moment a programme pauses, by requiring two full fiscal years of no requests before reversion, reported to Parliament. And Section 9 requires quarterly reporting on every release and disbursement, which for a billion-peso fund operating on ministry requests is the difference between a facility and a slush fund.

What the act cannot do is make reimbursement happen. It requires the MFBM to provide a mechanism for immediate reimbursement once national funds arrive, but nothing here reaches the national agency that is late in the first place. If the delays became permanent rather than occasional, the billion would drain and the act gives no answer to that.

readings.whatItDoes:
This moves the capital. The seat of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region is established at Parang in Maguindanao del Norte, where a new government centre is to be built to house the Office of the Wali, the Office of the Chief Minister, the Parliament, the ministries and agencies.

It is deliberately unhurried. A Committee on the Establishment of the Seat of Government — chaired by the Senior Minister, with the finance, public works, environment and transport ministers, the cultural heritage commission and the planning authority, and civil society organisations invited as observers — identifies the site, subject to Parliament's approval, and prepares the master plan and timetable. The physical transfer from Cotabato City proceeds gradually, only as office buildings, roads, light and power, water and communications are completed.

Two provisions deserve separate attention. Section 4 places the government centre outside local policies, measures and issuances that would run counter to the primacy of uninterrupted government service. And Section 7 requires the existing centre in Cotabato City to be improved rather than abandoned, preserved for its historical value, and renamed once the move is complete.

Fifty million pesos funds the first year, with foreign grants and donations permitted alongside the regional budget. The Committee dissolves when the job is done, and in any event within 10 years unless Parliament extends it.
readings.whyProposed: The act says only that the region has power to organise its own bureaucracy in the exercise of self-governance. It offers no stated reason for moving, and none for choosing Parang — which, for a decision of this magnitude, is a conspicuous silence.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Parang, whose municipality becomes the regional capital.
Cotabato City, which loses the seat of government it currently hosts.
Every government employee who would eventually relocate.
Anyone who travels to the regional government for services.
Local government units along the way, whom the Committee must consult.
implementedBy: Committee on the Establishment of the Seat of Government, chaired by the Senior Minister
Bangsamoro Parliament, which must approve the specific site
Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority and the ministries seated on the Committee

funding.detail: ₱50,000,000 for the Committee's first year, including the master plan, with later amounts through the General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro. Foreign grants, aid and donations may also be used, subject to Inter-Governmental Fiscal Policy Board guidelines. The act appropriates planning money; the cost of building a capital is nowhere estimated.

whatChanges: The region's seat of government moves from Cotabato City to Parang.
A planning committee with a ten-year life is created, with Parliament approving the site.
The new government centre sits partly outside local government authority.
The existing Cotabato City centre is preserved, improved and eventually renamed.
Foreign grants become an express funding channel.
readings.insight:
Cotabato City is the fact this act does not mention. It is not part of Maguindanao — it is a chartered city that voted in the 2019 plebiscite to join the Bangsamoro, and it has hosted the regional government ever since. Moving the seat to Parang relocates the capital out of that city and into the province. The act frames the whole thing as bureaucratic organisation and offers no reasoning, but the geography carries an argument the text declines to make.

Section 4 is the provision to watch. Excluding the government centre from local policies 'that would run counter to the primacy of uninterrupted government service' is drafted broadly enough to cover a great deal, and it creates an enclave of regional authority inside a municipality that is simultaneously promised consultation and dialogue. Which of those prevails in a real dispute is not answered here.

The design is otherwise careful in ways worth crediting. The transfer is conditioned on infrastructure actually existing rather than on a date, which avoids the standard failure of capital-moving projects — ministers decanted into a building site. Parliament must approve the site, so the choice of ground is not the executive's alone. Civil society is written in, if only as observers. And the old capital is to be preserved rather than left to decay, with its renaming treated as a matter for consultation. What is missing is a cost: fifty million pesos plans a capital, it does not build one, and the act never says what the real figure might be.

readings.whatItDoes:
This is about unpaid bills. Across three budget years the region had obligated money — committed it to contracts, to buildings, to goods delivered — and had not yet paid it out before the appropriations were due to die.

The act deals with each year in turn. For 2020 and 2021, infrastructure, capital outlays and continuing operating programmes could be obligated up to 31 December 2022; for 2022, up to 31 December 2023. And then, in each case, the same sentence: the appropriation shall continue to be effective until fully released and disbursed.

Personnel Services is excluded from all three, as in every act in this series — 2020 salary money died at the end of 2020, 2021's at the end of 2021, 2022's at the end of 2022. And the constituent LGUs' share of income taxes collected in the region is protected, available until fully expended or disbursed.
readings.whyProposed: To avoid leaving contractors and suppliers unpaid for work already done and accepted. An appropriation that lapses does not cancel the debt; it removes the legal authority to settle it, which is a worse outcome than an extension.
whoIsAffected: Contractors and suppliers owed for completed work under any of the three budgets.
Communities whose projects were funded and built but not yet paid for.
Constituent local government units, whose tax shares are protected.
Ministries and offices carrying unpaid obligations.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, authorised to issue implementing guidelines for each amended provision

funding.detail: No new appropriation and no amount stated. It keeps effective money already granted by BAA 3, BAA 15 and BAA 23.

whatChanges: Obligated amounts from 2020, 2021 and 2022 remain payable with no closing date.
New commitments were still bounded by the stated obligation cut-offs.
LGU income tax shares stay available until fully expended.
Salaries continue to expire on their original dates.
readings.insight:
This is the act that starts the shift, and it is worth being precise about the sequence. Read on its own it is unobjectionable — paying for work already delivered is the least controversial thing a budget law can do, and the alternative is stiffing contractors on a technicality. But the mechanism chosen was not another dated extension. It was the phrase 'shall continue to be effective until fully released and disbursed', applied to three budget years at once, in June 2023.

Six months later BAA 51 used comparable wording — 'until fully expended' — for the Special Development Fund, and BAA 52 carried it into the 2023 general appropriations. So the removal of disbursement deadlines was not a single decision about one pot of money; it began here, with unpaid obligations, and became the standing approach within half a year.

The distinction that keeps it defensible is one this act observes and the later ones partly relax: the open-ended wording applies to *disbursement of already-obligated amounts*, while the power to make new commitments still ends on a stated date. That is a meaningful line. An appropriation that can still pay old debts is not the same as one that can still be spent on new things. Anyone reading the region's budget legislation should check, in each act, which side of that line the open-ended clause sits on.

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the region deciding which days it stops for, and it distinguishes carefully between three kinds.

Four days are regular non-working holidays: Bangsamoro Foundation Day on 21 January, Eid'l Fit'r, Eid'l Adha, and the Day of Shuhada on 18 March. Two more are special non-working — the Day of Arafah and the first Day of Tashriq, both falling around the Hajj. Everything else is a special *working* holiday: commemorated, marked, funded, but not a day off.

That third category is where the region's history sits. Bud Daho on 6 March, Bayang on 2 May, Shariff Kabunsuan on 19 December, the signing of the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro on 27 March, and the 1996 Final Peace Agreement with the MNLF alongside the 1976 Tripoli Agreement on 2 September. Ministries, agencies and local governments must allocate funds and hold commemorative activities for them.

Because the Islamic dates move, Section 6 routes them through the Grand Mufti of the Bangsamoro Darul Ifta', who recommends the actual dates to the Chief Minister — and Section 11 requires the Chief Minister to publish the whole of next year's calendar by 31 December.

And Section 12 does the practical work: pending a Bangsamoro Labor Code, the holiday pay rules of the national Labor Code apply to private sector employees in the region.
readings.whyProposed: To replace Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 17, the ARMM-era law, with the region's own. The policy section names three things at once: preserving the heritage of the Bangsamoro *and other peoples* in the region, upholding the rights and well-being of workers, and keeping the regional economy competitive — which is a fair description of the tension every holiday law has to resolve.
whoIsAffected: Every private sector worker and employer in the region — the act binds the private sector expressly.
All regional government branches, agencies and instrumentalities, and constituent LGUs.
BARMM offices located outside the region, which are covered too.
Local governments wanting their own founding anniversary recognised.
Anyone whose legal deadline falls on a holiday.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister, which proclaims holidays and issues the annual calendar by 31 December
Grand Mufti of the Bangsamoro Darul Ifta', who recommends Islamic dates on the Hijri calendar
Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, which recommends localized proclamations and formulates guidelines
Ministries, agencies and LGUs, which must fund and conduct commemorative activities

funding.detail: No amount is stated. Section 8 requires every ministry, agency, office and LGU to allocate funds from their own budgets for activities commemorating the holidays.

whatChanges: The region has its own holiday law in place of the ARMM's.
Four regular and two special non-working holidays are fixed, with nine working commemorations.
An annual proclamation must publish next year's dates by 31 December.
Islamic dates are set through the Grand Mufti rather than administratively.
Private sector holiday compensation is expressly governed by the national Labor Code pending a regional one.
A deadline falling on a holiday moves to the next business day.
readings.insight:
The division between non-working and working holidays is where the act's real judgement lies, and it cuts in a particular direction. The days off are religious — the two Eids, Arafah, Tashriq — plus the region's founding and its martyrs. The battles, the treaties and the peace agreements are working holidays: commemorated with funded activities, but not at the cost of a day's production. The policy section's reference to the vibrance and competitiveness of the regional economy is doing visible work in that choice.

Section 12 is the quietly important one. A regional government can declare holidays; whether a worker is paid for them is labour law, and the Bangsamoro has not yet written its own. readings.whatItDoes:
This builds the region its own science high school system, and pegs it explicitly to the Philippine Science High School — the national specialist schools that are among the hardest places in the country to get into. Education in it is free to qualified Bangsamoro learners, and the Board may add scholarships, stipends and allowances on top.

The curriculum carries one element the national model does not: Values Education, defined in the act as a subject aimed at strengthening the foundations of faith among learners as they are trained in science and technology. The Mufti of the Bangsamoro Darul Ifta' sits on the Board of Trustees alongside the science and education ministers, the President of the Mindanao State University System, the chair of Parliament's science committee, two private sector representatives, and the president of the alumni association.

Money given to the System stays with it. Legacies and gifts are exempt from Bangsamoro taxes, and all revenues and donations go into a dedicated BSHS Fund used exclusively for the System's purposes.

The decision to peg the System to Philippine Science High School standards is the load-bearing one, and it cuts both ways. This act also spans two provinces' worth of local politics in miniature: it draws from Pikit and Aleosan, so two separate mother municipalities lose territory to it.

readings.whatItDoes:
This act creates a new municipality, Ligawasan, out of seven barangays that used to belong to Pikit in North Cotabato — Bagoinged, Barungis, Bulol, Buliok, Gli-Gli, Kabasalan, and Rajamuda. All seven voted in the 2019 plebiscite to join the Bangsamoro, and they sit in what the region calls its Special Geographic Areas. The act separates them from Pikit and constitutes them as a municipality in their own right, with its seat of government at Barangay Bagoinged and its boundary following the existing lines of the seven barangays.

Becoming a municipality is not automatic. The act requires a plebiscite in those barangays within 60 days of approval, run by the Commission on Elections through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office, and Ligawasan acquires corporate existence only if a majority of the votes cast approve. Until an election is held, the first mayor, vice-mayor, and council are appointed rather than elected.

A new municipality has no share of national tax revenue until it is entered into the allocation, so the act commits the Bangsamoro Government to pay monthly financial assistance for the new local government's administration and operation until that share arrives, subject to ordinary accounting and audit rules.
readings.whyProposed: The seven barangays voted in 2019 to leave North Cotabato for the Bangsamoro, which left them inside the region but still attached to a municipality outside it. The Bangsamoro Government has the power under the Organic Law to create municipalities, and this act uses it to give those barangays a local government of their own.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the seven barangays — about 29,800 people across roughly 112 square kilometres, by the figures annexed to the bill.
The Municipality of Pikit, North Cotabato, which loses the seven barangays and the revenue attached to them.
Elected officials of Pikit who live in the separated barangays: the bill addressed how their existing terms are handled.
The Bangsamoro Government, which carries the new municipality's operating cost until national tax allotment begins.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections, through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office, which conducts and supervises the plebiscite
The Bangsamoro Government, which appropriates the monthly financial assistance
The appointed first set of municipal officials, who run Ligawasan until an election is held

funding.detail: The bill as filed named a figure: not less than ₱2,500,000 every month until the municipality received its share of national tax revenue. The enacted act keeps the monthly commitment but drops the amount, promising financial assistance "every month" subject to usual accounting and auditing rules. Plebiscite costs come out of existing COMELEC funds.

whatChanges: Seven barangays stop being part of Pikit and become a municipality, if the plebiscite approves.
Ligawasan gains its own local government, seated at Bagoinged, initially by appointment rather than election.
The Bangsamoro Government takes on a recurring monthly cost until national tax allotment reaches the new municipality.
North Cotabato's Pikit is reduced by seven barangays, about 112 square kilometres.
readings.insight: The interesting difference is between the bill and the law. The filed copy guaranteed at least ₱2.5 million a month; the enacted text promises monthly assistance without saying how much. That converts a floor into a budget decision, and it is the kind of change that is invisible unless you read both documents. Worth tracking alongside it: the plebiscite had to happen within 60 days of approval, and a new municipality's finances stay dependent on the regional government until the national tax allotment catches up — which is a slower process than 60 days.

readings.whatItDoes:
This replaces the ARMM's local government code with the region's own, running to 605 sections across 4 Books and governing every province, city, municipality and barangay in the BARMM.

The structural commitment is devolution: ministries must gradually transfer basic services and facilities to LGUs within 5 years, supervised by a Devolution Committee chaired by the Senior Minister, which had 6 months to assess whether LGUs could actually carry them and 3 months more to produce a plan. Marawi City, Cotabato City and Basilan keep the full devolution status they already held.

On accountability, the Code does several things the national Local Government Code does not. Newly elected officials must complete 8 hours of onboarding and a 32-hour continuing programme that includes conflict-sensitivity and peacebuilding, with disqualification from the next election for those who deliberately skip it. Sanggunian members must disclose in writing any relationship within the 4th civil degree with anyone affected by a measure, before they take part in the debate. Sessions may be conducted in a local language. The interior ministry must maintain a Bangsamoro Register of Ordinances that is digital, online and public. A local treasurer who fails to publish monthly collections and disbursements faces a fine of ₱40,000 to ₱1,200,000, suspension or up to a year in prison.

And then Section 45(g), which is the provision everything else in this Code will be remembered alongside: anyone related within the 2nd civil degree to an incumbent local official running for office — parents, children, siblings, grandparents, grandchildren, and spouses — is disqualified from running in the same election in that same province, city, municipality or barangay. Every candidate must swear in their certificate of candidacy that no such relationship exists.
readings.whyProposed: The region had inherited the ARMM's 1990s code and needed one built for a parliamentary regional government with 15 ministries and a devolution timetable. The accountability provisions answer a more specific problem, one the Code's own transitory section is candid about: local office in this region has tended to stay in a small number of families.
whoIsAffected: Every voter and every candidate for local office in the region.
All constituent provinces, cities, municipalities and barangays.
Ratepayers and taxpayers, through the local taxation Book.
Residents of the Special Geographic Area, now organised into 8 municipalities.
Barangay officials, tanods and peacekeeping teams, newly covered by insurance.
Communities in the path of regional projects, protected by consultation and relocation requirements.
implementedBy: Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, through its Local Government Operations Officers
Devolution Committee, chaired by the Senior Minister, with parliamentary and LGU representation
Office of the Chief Minister, exercising general supervision and disciplinary jurisdiction over senior local officials
Bangsamoro Local Government Academy, delivering the mandatory training
Bangsamoro Electoral Office of the COMELEC, on plebiscites, recall and candidate eligibility
Special Geographic Area Development Authority, attached to the Office of the Chief Minister

funding.detail: ₱10,000,000 initially, charged against the appropriations of the Office of the Chief Minister, for the Devolution Committee's work including an information campaign on the Code. LGU operations are funded from their share of national taxes and their own revenue-raising powers under Book II, with the Bangsamoro Government providing assistance and augmentation at no extra cost to the LGU.

whatChanges: The ARMM's local government code is repealed and replaced.
Basic services devolve from regional ministries to LGUs over 5 years.
Elected officials must be trained, and can be disqualified for refusing.
Close relatives of incumbents are barred from the same ballot, from 2028.
A public digital register of every local ordinance is created.
The 63 Special Geographic Area barangays become 8 municipalities with their own taxing powers.
readings.insight:
Section 45(g) is the most ambitious thing this Code attempts, and Section 595 is the sentence that determines what it will actually mean. The Philippines has had an anti-dynasty clause in its Constitution since 1987 and no enabling law in the four decades since; Congress has never passed one. A regional legislature enacting one for its own local offices is genuinely without precedent in the country. And then the transitory provision defers it — along with the training disqualification — to the May 2028 elections, 5 years after the Code took effect and a full local election cycle away.

There are defensible reasons to phase in a rule that reshapes who may stand for office: candidates and families need notice, and the electoral machinery needs time to administer a relationship test. But the effect is that the officials who passed the Code did not have to run under it, and the 2025 local elections proceeded on the old rules. Whether the provision survives to 2028 is a live question — Section 586 says the Code may only be amended after the mandatory review, but that review falls 10 years after enactment, in 2033, which either entrenches Section 45(g) against early repeal or will simply be worked around.

The scope is also worth reading carefully rather than from the headline. The bar reaches the 2nd civil degree — parents, children, siblings, spouses — and only relatives of an *incumbent running in the same election*, in the *same* LGU. A family can still hold the governorship and a mayoralty in different municipalities. A relative can run once the incumbent steps back. Cousins, nephews and in-laws beyond the second degree are untouched. Paragraphs (h) and (i) close two adjacent doors — an incumbent cannot decamp to run in a neighbouring LGU, and a chief executive cannot step down to the next office below — which suggests the drafters were thinking about the actual manoeuvres, not just the principle.

What the Code does immediately, and without deferral, is smaller but real: disclosure of conflicts before a sanggunian member debates a measure; a digital public register of ordinances; criminal liability for a treasurer who stops publishing the monthly numbers; sessions in a local language with minutes translated; insurance for the barangay tanod. Those are the provisions a resident might actually use next week, and they arrived in 2023.

One quiet asymmetry runs through the whole Code, as it does through the Administrative Code. Section 33 governs local chief executives' supervision over the police, fire and jail personnel in their jurisdiction by referring the question entirely to “applicable national law and the BOL”. The region wrote 605 sections about local government and left the one about who controls the police at a cross-reference.

readings.whatItDoes:
This takes the ARMM-era Regional Madrasah Graduate Academy at Buluan, abolishes its 2003 charter, and rebuilds it as a chartered regional institution of higher learning — the Bangsamoro Kulliyyah for Islamic Studies — offering baccalaureate and postgraduate degrees in Islamic studies and Arabic.

The governance is the notable part. A Board of Trustees chaired by the education Minister holds the highest policy-making power, and its membership reaches well beyond officialdom: the president of the faculty association, the president of the Student Government Organization, the president of the Alumni Association, a representative of private Islamic institutions recognised by the ministry, and the Bangsamoro Mufti all sit on it as members.

Financially it is given something most attached agencies are not: its own money. Tuition, fees, government subsidies and income from auxiliary services and land grants become special trust funds that the Kulliyyah retains and the Board disburses, with interest staying in the fund. Donations to it are exempt from all taxes and deductible from the donor's income tax. Against that, the Board must run a socialised tuition scheme for poor but deserving students.

And Section 19, in a single sentence, says the Kulliyyah shall not discriminate on the basis of colour, race, religion, sex or disability in admissions, employment or any programme.
readings.whyProposed: The academy was operating under a twenty-year-old ARMM statute. A region committed to an educational system that is “a subsystem of the national education system” needed an institution that could actually award recognised degrees in Islamic and Arabic studies, rather than an academy whose graduates' credentials sat awkwardly against the national framework.
whoIsAffected: Madrasah graduates seeking degree-level study.
Students, faculty and alumni, each with a seat on the governing board.
Private Islamic institutions recognised by the education ministry.
Personnel of the defunct REMAcademy, transitioned within 90 days.
Communities elsewhere in the region, where branches may be opened.
implementedBy: Board of Trustees, chaired by the Minister of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, meeting at least quarterly
Office of the President of the Kulliyyah, appointed by the Chief Minister from at least three Board-endorsed nominees for a four-year term renewable once
Academic Council, chaired by the President and composed of academic staff at Assistant Professor rank and above
MBHTE, holding direct supervision, regulatory powers, the staffing pattern and the implementing rules

funding.detail: No peso figure is appropriated. Initial implementation is charged against the current year's appropriations, and continued operation and maintenance is carried in the education ministry's budget under the annual appropriations act. The institution's own tuition, fees, subsidies, auxiliary service income and land grant income are retained as special trust funds it may disburse itself.

whatChanges: The region gains a chartered institution awarding degrees in Islamic studies and Arabic.
Students, faculty and alumni take seats on its governing board.
The institution keeps and spends its own tuition and income.
Socialised tuition becomes a requirement, and discrimination on religion or disability is barred.
The Regional Madrasah Graduate Education Act of 2003 is repealed and the academy absorbed.
readings.insight:
Section 19 is the sentence to notice, because of where it appears. An institution created specifically for Islamic studies, with the Bangsamoro Mufti on its board, is told in plain terms that it may not discriminate on the basis of religion in admissions, employment or any programme. Read alongside BAA 64's direction that the Tribal University shall be open to all “regardless of religion, ethnicity or nationality” while prioritising indigenous learners, a consistent drafting instinct shows through: the region builds institutions rooted in a particular community and then writes the door open. Whether that reflects conviction or a careful eye on the constitutional limits of a subsystem of the national education system, the effect is the same.

The financial design is the other thing worth pulling out, and it is unusually generous by the standards of this registry. Most bodies created by these acts get a peso figure and then depend on the annual budget. This one gets no figure at all — but it gets to keep its own money. Tuition, fees, subsidies, auxiliary income, land grant income, and the interest on all of it, become special trust funds the Board disburses “any provision of existing laws, rules, and regulations to the contrary notwithstanding”. Donations come in tax-free and leave the donor's income tax lighter. For an institution expected to build itself up, that combination is worth more than a one-off appropriation — provided it can attract enough students and donors to make the retention meaningful, which for a specialised institution in Buluan is not a small proviso.

Where the autonomy stops is equally clear. The education ministry chairs the Board, holds direct supervision and regulatory powers, and determines the complete staffing pattern. The Chief Minister appoints the President — from the Board's shortlist, but the choice is not the Board's — and appoints everyone at Salary Grade 25 and above. The President sits at Salary Grade 26, below the head of any of the region's commissions, and below several division chiefs elsewhere in the bureaucracy. An institution can be given its own money and its own board and still be quite firmly held; this one is.

readings.whatItDoes:
This does two things, and the second matters far more than the first.

The first is routine: it moves deadlines. Special Development Fund money from 2020, 2021 and 2022 can be released and obligated until 31 December 2024; money from the 2023 fund until 31 December 2025. Four budget years of development spending, extended in one act.

The second is a change of kind rather than degree. Each of the three provisions ends with the same phrase — the appropriations 'shall continue to be available for disbursement until fully expended'. That removes the payment deadline altogether. Under a cash budgeting system an appropriation dies on a date whether or not it has been spent; under this wording, the money for these four funds does not die at all. It ends when it runs out.
readings.whyProposed: Projects funded from four successive Special Development Funds were unfinished, and the earlier extension in BAA 34 was itself expiring. Rather than return year after year for another date, Parliament removed the date.
whoIsAffected: Communities whose development projects draw on any Special Development Fund from 2020 onward.
Contractors, for whom payment is no longer bounded by a statutory deadline.
Ministries and offices administering the funds.
Bangsamoro taxpayers, whose money is now held under a materially weaker time constraint.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, authorised to issue guidelines for the cash budgeting system

funding.detail: No new appropriation and no amounts stated. It extends funds appropriated by BAA 22 (₱10 billion for 2020–2021), BAA 23 (2022) and BAA 32 (2023).

whatChanges: Release and obligation windows extended to end-2024, and to end-2025 for the 2023 fund.
The disbursement deadline is removed for all 4 years — the money is available until fully expended.
The underlying appropriations acts otherwise remain in force.
readings.insight:
Follow the chain and the shape of it is clear. BAA 22 appropriated ₱10 billion under a cash budgeting rule with hard dates. BAA 14 and 24 extended the general budgets, always keeping outer limits. BAA 34 extended this fund with staged deadlines — obligate by end-2023, pay by mid-2024. And this act extends it again and takes the payment deadline away entirely.

The wording did not originate here. BAA 38, 6 months earlier, had already made the 2020–2022 general appropriations 'effective until fully released and disbursed' — but only for amounts already obligated, to settle unpaid bills. This act goes further: it removes the limit on the fund's availability itself, not merely on paying debts already incurred.

'Until fully expended' is four words that undo the central discipline of the system the region wrote for itself. A deadline is what forces an agency either to spend money on the thing it was voted for or to give it back to be voted again; without one, an appropriation can sit obligated indefinitely, and the question of whether the project was ever delivered stops having a date attached to it. Note also what is not here: no reporting duty, no progress requirement, no review — none of the quarterly publication machinery that BAA 33 imposed on the general budget a year earlier reaches these funds.

There is a real argument on the other side, and the registry should state it. A post-conflict government building roads and clinics from nothing, through a pandemic, with procurement capacity it was still constructing, cannot deliver on an annual cash cycle — and repeated short extensions are their own kind of waste, consuming parliamentary time and leaving contractors uncertain. Removing the deadline is the honest version of what the previous three acts were doing anyway.

But it is a decision about accountability, made in a sentence at the end of three subsections, in an act whose title says only that it continues validity. Anyone tracking where the region's development money actually goes should treat this as one of the most consequential provisions in the registry.

readings.whatItDoes:
On its face this is another budget extension: the 2023 appropriations stay releasable and obligable to the end of 2024, with obligated infrastructure and operating items valid until fully expended, and anything unreleased lapsing back to the Treasury for reappropriation.

But buried in the same section is a definition that does real work. Funds transferred between organisational units within a ministry, between ministries, or from a ministry to a local government unit are *not considered disbursed* until the transferred amounts have actually been used to pay for completed construction, goods delivered and services rendered — inspected and accepted, within the validity period.

And one protection is carved out above everything else: notwithstanding any other provision or issuance, the shares of constituent LGUs in national taxes collected in the region remain available until fully released, obligated and disbursed.
readings.whyProposed: The 2023 appropriations were expiring. Parliament took the occasion to write into the budget's general provisions a rule about what spending actually means.
whoIsAffected: Communities and contractors with 2023-funded works.
Constituent local government units, whose tax shares are protected from lapse.
Every ministry, office and agency, whose reported disbursements now have a statutory test to meet.
Anyone reading Bangsamoro spending figures.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, authorised to issue guidelines for the cash budgeting system

funding.detail: No new appropriation and no amount stated. It extends money already granted by BAA 32 for fiscal year 2023.

whatChanges: The 2023 budget runs a year longer, with obligated items valid until fully expended.
Transfers between units, or to LGUs, no longer count as disbursement.
LGU shares of national taxes are protected until fully released, obligated and disbursed.
Personnel Services and General Administration and Support MOOE expire at the end of 2023.
The Special Development Fund is expressly carved out to its own law.
readings.insight:
The transfer clause is the single most technically astute provision in the region's budget legislation, and it addresses a manoeuvre anyone who has watched public spending will recognise. When an appropriation is about to lapse, the easiest way to 'spend' it is to move it — to another organisational unit, to another ministry, or best of all to a local government unit, where it sits in an account while the transferring agency reports the money as disbursed and the deadline is satisfied. Nothing has been built. The money has simply changed hands.

This act says that does not count. Disbursement happens when the money pays for completed construction, goods delivered or services rendered, inspected and accepted — not when it is handed on. That converts a reporting formality back into a question about whether anything was actually delivered, and it does so in one sentence.

Set against BAA 51, passed the very same day, the pairing is striking. That act removed the disbursement deadline for the Special Development Fund entirely; this one tightened what disbursement means for the general budget. Parliament loosened the constraint on one pot of money and sharpened the definition governing another, in a single sitting — and Section 50-A here is what keeps the two regimes separate, expressly leaving the Development Fund to its own law.

readings.whatItDoes:
This takes nineteen barangays out of the Municipality of Sultan Kudarat and makes them a municipality of their own, to be called Nuling, seated at Barangay Pinaring — which the act renames the Poblacion.

Nothing happens on signature. Section 5 makes corporate existence depend on a plebiscite: a majority of the votes cast by qualified voters in those nineteen barangays, held within 60 days of approval, run by COMELEC and paid for out of the region's Contingent Fund under the 2024 budget. Until that vote, Nuling exists only on paper.

If it passes, the Chief Minister appoints the first mayor, vice-mayor and eight council members, who hold office until the next regular election. And because a new municipality has no tax base until the national revenue allotment reaches it, the Bangsamoro Government must provide not less than ₱2.5 million every month to run it in the meantime.
readings.whyProposed: The Organic Law gives the region power to redraw its own local government map — creating, dividing, merging or abolishing municipalities and barangays by act of Parliament — subject in every case to ratification by the people directly affected. This is that power being used.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the nineteen named barangays, who both vote on the change and live with the result.
Residents of what remains of Sultan Kudarat, the mother municipality, which loses nineteen barangays.
Incumbent Sangguniang Bayan members of Sultan Kudarat who live in the new municipality — they finish their terms serving the mother municipality, not the new one.
Bangsamoro taxpayers, who fund ₱2.5 million a month until the revenue allotment arrives.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections, which conducts and supervises the plebiscite
Office of the Chief Minister, which appoints the first municipal officials
Bangsamoro Government, which appropriates the monthly financial assistance

funding.detail: Not less than ₱2,500,000 every month for the administration and operation of the new municipal government, until it is allocated its share in the revenue allotment. The plebiscite itself is charged to the BARMM Contingent Fund under the fiscal year 2024 appropriations. At that floor the assistance runs to at least ₱30 million a year.

whatChanges: Nineteen barangays leave Sultan Kudarat and form a distinct and independent municipality, if the plebiscite passes.
A new local government is seated at Pinaring, closer to the people it serves.
The municipality becomes entitled to its own share of national taxes.
A monthly subsidy floor of ₱2.5 million bridges the gap until that share arrives.
readings.insight:
The plebiscite is the act's own check on itself, and it is worth noticing how narrowly it is drawn. The vote is held only in the barangays being carved out — the people leaving Sultan Kudarat decide, and those staying behind do not. Section 1 speaks of 'the political units directly affected', and the act reads that as the departing barangays alone, even though the mother municipality loses nineteen barangays and whatever revenue they represent.

The appointment provision is the other thing a reader should not skim past. A municipality created to bring government closer to its people begins with a mayor, a vice-mayor and eight councillors none of whom its people chose; all ten are appointed by the Chief Minister and serve until the next regular election. That is a defensible transitional arrangement — there is no other way to stand up a local government mid-cycle — but it means the first act of a new municipality's self-government is performed by someone in Cotabato City.

What the act does not contain is any measure of the thing it creates. No land area, no population, no revenue projection, and no statement of why nineteen barangays rather than some other number. The ₱2.5 million monthly floor is the only number in it, and nothing in the text lets a reader judge whether that is generous or thin for the population involved.

readings.whatItDoes:
Thirteen barangays — Tapian, Linek, Dinaig Proper, Tamontaka, Tanuel, Kusiong, Mompong, Semba, Capiton, Tambak, Badak, Awang and Dulangan — leave the Municipality of Datu Odin Sinsuat and become the Municipality of Datu Sinsuat Balabaran, seated at Tamontaka.

This is the most carefully surveyed of the three creations passed that day. It gives a land area to the square metre — 143,984,505, about 144 square kilometres — and, alone among them, annexes a full technical description of the boundary as Annex 1b. Where its siblings say the boundary follows the existing barangay lines and stop, this one attaches the survey.

The rest follows the template: corporate existence on ratification by plebiscite within 60 days, run by COMELEC and paid from the Contingent Fund; a mayor, vice-mayor and eight councillors appointed by the Chief Minister; and not less than ₱2.5 million a month from the Bangsamoro Government until the municipality receives its share of national taxes.
readings.whyProposed: The Organic Law's power to redraw the region's local government map, exercised on the same day for three municipalities in Maguindanao del Norte.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the thirteen named barangays.
Datu Odin Sinsuat, which loses thirteen barangays here and ten more to BAA 55 on the same day.
Incumbent councillors of Datu Odin Sinsuat living in the new municipality.
Bangsamoro taxpayers, funding ₱2.5 million a month.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections, which conducts and supervises the plebiscite
Office of the Chief Minister, which appoints the first municipal officials
Bangsamoro Government, which appropriates the monthly financial assistance

funding.detail: Not less than ₱2,500,000 every month until the municipality is allocated its internal revenue allotment share — at that floor, at least ₱30 million a year. The plebiscite is charged to the BARMM Contingent Fund under the fiscal year 2024 appropriations.

whatChanges: Thirteen barangays leave Datu Odin Sinsuat and form a distinct and independent municipality, if the plebiscite passes.
A surveyed boundary is fixed by annexed technical description.
A monthly subsidy floor bridges the gap until national tax share arrives.
readings.insight:
Read this beside BAA 55 and the scale of what happened to one municipality becomes clear. Datu Odin Sinsuat lost thirteen barangays to this act and ten more to the Sheik Abas Hamza act, both passed on 20 December 2023 and approved on the same day — twenty-three barangays in a single sitting, and neither act mentions the other. Nothing in either text says what is left of the mother municipality, what its remaining population or revenue would be, or whether anyone assessed the combined effect.

That matters because of how the plebiscite was originally drawn. Both acts, as enacted, polled only the departing barangays. The municipality losing twenty-three of them had no vote in either. Parliament came back a year later and amended both — BAA 70 for this act, BAA 71 for its sibling — to hold the plebiscite in 'the political units directly affected', which is the Organic Law's own formula and is ordinarily read to include the mother unit. The correction is the strongest evidence that the original drafting was understood to be wrong.

The technical description annexed here is the act's one clear advantage over its siblings. In a region where boundary disputes are neither academic nor rare, attaching the survey rather than gesturing at existing barangay lines is the difference between a boundary and an argument.

readings.whatItDoes:
Ten barangays — Labungan, Taviran, Baka, Sapalan, Sifaran, Bugawas, Bitu, Kurintem, Margues and Makir — leave the Municipality of Datu Odin Sinsuat and become a municipality of their own, named for Sheik Abas Hamza and seated at Barangay Bugawas.

The act is more precise about the ground than its siblings: it states a land area of 164,387,474 square metres, about 164 square kilometres, with the boundary following the existing barangay lines.

As with the other creations, none of it happens without a vote. A majority of the votes cast by qualified voters in those ten barangays, within 60 days of approval, run and supervised by COMELEC and paid for from the region's Contingent Fund. If it passes, the Chief Minister appoints the first mayor, vice-mayor and eight councillors, and the Bangsamoro Government pays not less than ₱2.5 million a month to run the place until its share of national taxes arrives.
readings.whyProposed: The same Organic Law power to redraw the region's local government map, exercised on the same day as the Nuling and Datu Sinsuat Balabaran creations — three new municipalities carved out of Maguindanao del Norte in a single sitting.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the ten named barangays, who vote on the change and live with the result.
Residents of what remains of Datu Odin Sinsuat, which loses ten barangays.
Incumbent councillors of Datu Odin Sinsuat living in the new municipality, who finish their terms in the mother municipality.
Bangsamoro taxpayers, funding ₱2.5 million a month until the revenue allotment arrives.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections, which conducts and supervises the plebiscite
Office of the Chief Minister, which appoints the first municipal officials
Bangsamoro Government, which appropriates the monthly financial assistance

funding.detail: Not less than ₱2,500,000 every month until the municipality is allocated its Internal Revenue Allotment share — at that floor, at least ₱30 million a year. The plebiscite is charged to the BARMM Contingent Fund under the fiscal year 2024 appropriations.

whatChanges: Ten barangays leave Datu Odin Sinsuat and form a distinct and independent municipality, if the plebiscite passes.
A new local government is seated at Bugawas.
The municipality becomes entitled to its own share of national taxes.
A monthly subsidy floor of ₱2.5 million bridges the gap until that share arrives.
readings.insight:
Three municipalities were created out of Maguindanao del Norte on 1 day, each on the same template and each carrying the same ₱2.5 million monthly floor. That is at least ₱90 million a year in bridging subsidy committed in a single sitting, before any of the three has a tax base — and the acts are silent on how long that bridge is expected to be, because the Internal Revenue Allotment share depends on a national allocation cycle none of them controls.

This one is the most carefully surveyed of the three: it is the only one to state a land area. Section 4 gives it to the square metre — 164,387,474 — which is a precision worth noting in a region where boundary disputes are not academic. What none of the three states is population, which is the figure that would tell a reader whether ₱2.5 million a month is generous or inadequate.

And this act did not stay as passed. Section 5, the plebiscite requirement, was subsequently amended by BAA 71 — so anyone relying on the ratification timetable in this text should read that amendment alongside it.

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the region's budget for 2024 — ₱98,467,200,000.00, a 15.4% jump on the year before, published under the theme “Accelerating Structural Reforms, Boosting Sustainable Development, and Enhancing Human Capital in the Bangsamoro”.

The money comes from the annual block grant, other national subsidies, the region's share of national taxes collected inside its territory, projected collections on its own taxes and fees, and two categories of money the government already had: unutilized prior years' appropriations, and unutilized prior year's allotments reverted to the Treasury.

It funds 17 ministries, 11 other executive offices and 6 special purpose funds. The Bangsamoro Transition Authority receives ₱4,831,206,302, about 4.9% of the total. Local governments do markedly better than before: the Local Government Support Fund nearly triples to ₱6,536,000,000, and a new ₱2,033,183,600 line appears for their share of taxes collected within the region.

But the change that matters most is in Section 49. Every Bangsamoro budget until this one expired after a single year, and every one of them had to be rescued by a separate act the following December — BAA 14, BAA 24, BAA 33, BAA 52, four laws whose only job was to extend a budget that had run out of time. This act gives itself 2 years. Appropriations stay available for release and obligation until 31 December 2025; Personnel Services and General Administration and Support running costs still expire at the end of 2024; and anything obligated by the end of 2025 for construction, goods or services stays “valid until fully expended”. Local government transfers do not lapse at all.

The familiar rules carry over: Personnel Services capped at 45% of total revenue, at least 5% of every agency's budget for gender and development, engineering and administrative overhead held to 1% on projects over ₱1,000,000, a ₱5,000 floor under monthly net take-home pay, published contracts and actual costs for every infrastructure project, and automatic salary suspension for officials who miss their accountability reports.

One long-standing provision is gone. Hazard duty pay for personnel in “strife-torn or embattled areas”, granted in every budget since the region's first, does not appear here.
readings.whyProposed: The Bangsamoro Government needs an annual appropriations act to function. This one was passed on 21 December 2023 and signed by the Chief Minister on 29 December, 3 days before it took effect. Its cover sets out the theme as an acronym — A for Accelerating, B for Boosting, E for Enhancing — the initials of Chief Minister Ahod Balawag Ebrahim. The FY 2025 budget carries the same theme.
whoIsAffected: Everyone in the region served by a Bangsamoro Government programme.
Constituent local government units, whose transfers rise sharply and no longer expire.
All government personnel, whose representation and clothing allowances rise.
Personnel who had been receiving hazard duty pay, which this act drops.
Contractors, who now have a second year to complete and be paid for projects.
Women's programmes, guaranteed a 5% share of every agency budget.
implementedBy: All 17 ministries, the 11 other executive offices and the special purpose funds
Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, administering releases and issuing guidelines
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, on transfers to local governments
Ministry of Public Works, setting infrastructure standards
Bangsamoro Women Commission, on gender and development plans
Commission on Audit, as external auditor

funding.detail: ₱98,467,200,000.00 for fiscal year 2024, from the annual block grant, other subsidies from the National Government, the region's share of national taxes, fees and charges collected in its territorial jurisdiction, unutilized prior years' appropriations from the Bangsamoro Treasury, unutilized prior year's allotments reverted to the Bangsamoro Treasury, and projected collections on regional taxes, fees and charges. Personnel Services across government are capped at 45% of total revenue sources. BAA 63 added ₱8,441,261,975 in supplemental funds in September 2024.

whatChanges: ₱98.47 billion is appropriated for 2024, a 15.4% increase on the year before.
The budget runs 2 years instead of 1, ending the annual extension acts.
Local government transfers rise to ₱8.57 billion across two lines and stop lapsing.
Representation and transportation allowances rise for every rank; clothing allowance rises to ₱7,000.
Hazard duty pay for strife-torn areas is dropped without explanation.
The Contingent Fund falls to ₱3.78 billion, 3.8% of the budget.
readings.insight:
Four separate laws exist for no reason other than that a Bangsamoro budget ran out of time. BAA 14 extended FY 2020. BAA 24 extended FY 2020 and FY 2021 together. BAA 33 extended FY 2022. BAA 52 extended FY 2023. Each was passed in the same December week as the next year's budget, each pushed an expiring appropriation out by 12 months, and each was an admission that the government could not spend within the year what Parliament had given it.

Section 49 of this act ends that. The appropriations run to 31 December 2025; obligated capital outlays and goods and services stay valid “until fully expended”; and local government transfers do not lapse at all. There is no extension act for FY 2024, because there did not need to be one. That is a real reform, and it is the clearest thing the theme's promise of “structural reforms” actually delivered.

It is also an accommodation rather than a cure. The same Section 1 that names the total lists two sources that only exist because money went unspent — “unutilized prior years' appropriations” and, new this year, “unutilized prior year's allotments reverted to the Bangsamoro Treasury”. And 9 months into the fiscal year, BAA 63 appropriated another ₱8,441,261,975 in supplemental funds, drawn from the same pool of previously unspent money. Giving the money two years to be spent removes the annual embarrassment of the extension act; it does not, by itself, get the money spent.

The Contingent Fund tells the underlying story better than any single provision. It was ₱13.2 billion in FY 2020, 20% of the entire budget. Here it is ₱3,775,038,731, or 3.8%. Over the same period the Local Government Support Fund went from nothing to ₱6.54 billion, and a further ₱2.03 billion was carved out as the constituent LGUs' tax share. The region has been steadily converting a large discretionary reserve into formula-driven transfers with named recipients — which is what a maturing budget looks like.

Against that, two figures have not moved since 2020. PERA is still ₱2,000 a month and the floor under an employee's monthly net take-home pay is still ₱5,000, while representation and transportation allowances rose this year for every rank from the Chief Minister down. The allowances attached to office were adjusted; the floor protecting the lowest-paid was not.

And hazard duty pay is simply absent. From FY 2020 through FY 2023 the general provisions granted it to personnel serving in “strife-torn or embattled areas as may be determined and certified by the Secretary of National Defense”. There is no repealing clause and no explanation — the section is just not there, and it has not returned in any budget since.

readings.whatItDoes:
This pays a pension. A Mujahideen of the MILF or the MNLF who fought for at least 20 years between 1969 and 2014, who is now a senior citizen or permanently disabled, and whose income is under ₱250,000 a year, receives ₱7,000 every month for the rest of their life.

The first year comes as a single payment of ₱84,000 covering the whole 12 months; after that it is released quarterly. The benefit is lifetime and non-transferrable — it stops at death and does not pass to a family.

To run it the act creates an office inside the Office of the Chief Minister, the Office of the Bangsamoro Mujahideen Under Special Circumstance, headed by a Director II and split into 3 sections: one that processes and validates claims, one that handles availment, and one that monitors and evaluates. It must keep an updated register of who qualifies, and every 3 years it must review whether ₱7,000 is still enough to live on.
readings.whyProposed: The act's policy section puts it as the Bangsamoro Government's duty to see that every Bangsamoro has basic necessities and equal opportunities, with economic mechanisms tailored to its people's needs. The specific gap it fills is a generation of combatants who gave two decades to the struggle and arrived at old age or permanent disability with no income and no pension of any kind.
whoIsAffected: Male and female members of the MILF and MNLF — the act says both expressly — who meet all three tests: 20 years of meaningful participation between 1969 and 2014, senior citizen status or permanent disability, and an annual income no higher than ₱250,000.

Anyone whose disability is on the act's list: partial covers the loss of use of a finger, arm, foot, toe, hand, leg, one or both ears, hearing, or the sight of one eye; total covers blindness in both eyes, the loss of two limbs at or above the ankle or wrists, paralysis of two limbs, and brain injury causing incurable incapacity.
The Central Committees of the MILF and the MNLF, which supply the list of qualified and validated beneficiaries and so decide, in practice, who gets on it.
Families of beneficiaries, who inherit nothing: the pension is non-transferrable.
implementedBy: Office of the Bangsamoro Mujahideen Under Special Circumstance (OBMUSC), headed by a Director II appointed by the Chief Minister for 3 years
Office of the Chief Minister, which holds operational supervision and control over the OBMUSC
A technical working group formed by the OCM with the Committee on Social Services and Development, which had 90 days from effectivity to issue implementing rules
The Central Committees of the MILF and the MNLF, which validate the beneficiary list

funding.detail: ₱500,000,000 appropriated for initial implementation upon effectivity. Continuing costs are carried in the annual General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro under the Office of the Chief Minister. At ₱84,000 a head in the first year, the initial appropriation is the size of roughly 5,950 full-year pensions — the act does not state how many people are expected to qualify.

whatChanges: A lifetime pension exists where there was none: ₱7,000 a month, ₱84,000 in the first year.
A dedicated office is created inside the Office of the Chief Minister to validate, pay and monitor.
For the first time there is a register of qualified Mujahideen, built with the MILF and MNLF central committees.
The adequacy of the amount is put on a three-year review cycle rather than left to erode.
readings.insight:
The eligibility gate is the whole act. Three tests have to be met at once — 20 years of participation inside a fixed 1969–2014 window, old age or a listed disability, and an income ceiling of ₱250,000 — and the act never says how any of it is proved. It routes validation to the Central Committees of the MILF and the MNLF instead. That is a practical answer to a hard problem: no state record exists of who fought. It also means a former combatant's pension depends on a list drawn up by a political organisation, and the act provides no appeal if a name is left off it.

The money is worth doing arithmetic on. ₱500 million is the initial appropriation, and the first-year benefit is ₱84,000 a head, which funds roughly 5,950 people for that year. The act does not estimate the eligible population, so whether that figure is generous or thin is unanswerable from the text alone — and the answer decides whether this reads as a pension scheme or as a pilot.

Two smaller things. The benefit stops at death and cannot pass to a widow or children, which for a household living on ₱7,000 a month is a cliff rather than a step. And the act creates no offence — there is no penalty for a fraudulent claim, only validation standing between the register and the money.

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the map. Before the Bangsamoro can elect district representatives, someone has to say where the districts are — and this act says it, in 7 pages of municipalities and barangays with a population beside each one.

Thirty-two single-member districts. Lanao del Sur takes eight, Sulu seven, the two Maguindanao provinces four each, Basilan and Tawi-Tawi three each, Cotabato City two, and the Special Geographic Area a single Lone District covering all eight of its municipalities. The stated regional population is 4,944,800.

The criteria in Section 3 are conventional and, importantly, published: apportionment on population and geographical area; districts to be contiguous, compact and adjacent territory as far as practicable; and a floor of 100,000 people per district. Every district's population is printed alongside it, so the arithmetic can be checked against the rule.
readings.whyProposed: The Organic Law provides for a Parliament partly elected from districts. Until the districts existed in law, there was nothing for a district representative to be elected from. This is the foundational piece of the region's electoral architecture.
whoIsAffected: Every voter in the region, whose district is fixed here.
Candidates, whose constituency boundaries this defines.
Municipalities and, in Cotabato City, individual barangays, grouped into constituencies.
The Special Geographic Area, whose eight municipalities are given one collective seat.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections, through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office, which administers elections on this map

funding.detail: The act appropriates nothing. It draws boundaries.

whatChanges: The region acquires a defined electoral map for the first time.
Every municipality and Cotabato City barangay is assigned to a district.
A population floor of 100,000 per district is set.
The Special Geographic Area gains representation as a single constituency.
readings.insight:
The most consequential decision in the act is the one that looks least like a decision: the Special Geographic Area gets one district for 215,433 people, while the floor for any district is 100,000. On population alone the SGA would support 2 seats. Instead its eight municipalities — territory that voted into the region in 2019 and had to be organised into municipalities the year before this act — vote as a single constituency, with a population more than double the smallest districts elsewhere. Nothing in the act explains why, and for a population whose incorporation into the region is itself recent, the difference between 1 seat and two is not a technicality.

The published population figures are the act's real contribution to accountability. Districts range from about 111,000 to over 207,000, which is a wide spread for a map drawn on a 100,000 floor, and because every figure is printed the spread is checkable by anyone. Legislatures redistricting themselves do not always leave that evidence lying about.

Two further things a reader should carry away. The act was passed and approved by the Chief Minister on the same day, which is fast for a measure of this significance. And this map did not hold: BAA 77 reconstituted the districts in 2025 and BAA 86 re-apportioned them in 2026, so anyone working out which district they vote in should start with those acts and use this one as the baseline they revised.
